title: Local by Default, Escalated by Rule
author: Stefan Norrvall
summary: Stefan Norrvall argues that large organisations can describe how work should be done but cannot say who owns a given class of decision, when it leaves them, or what happens if nobody decides. The usual remedy of pushing decisions as far down as possible fails because possible is undefined, local roles lack the authority to make decisions stick, and the work itself is not one thing. He proposes that a decision belongs with the closest role that can bear the consequences, reach the evidence and hold real authority within explicit thresholds, and that it escalates only when a rule written in advance says so. A software-release example shows the same people and the same decision taking eleven working days in one organisation and a morning in another. He offers five placement questions, argues that the default for a stalled decision should be named rather than left to the status quo, and lists four conditions that make local authority credible to executives and regulators.
points: Decisions stall because no one can say whose they are, so they travel up for comfort, sideways for consensus and into forums for cover.
Pushing decisions down fails when possible is undefined, when local roles lack authority to commit, and when close to the work is not specified.
A decision stays local when the role can bear the consequences, reach the evidence and hold authority within explicit thresholds; otherwise a written trigger moves it.
Five questions on outcome, authority, decision type, transfer threshold and stall behaviour tell a leader where a decision belongs and what is missing.
Local authority is credible when thresholds are testable, material decisions are recorded, waivers expire and a named role arbitrates between authorities.
quotes: A decision that should take a day takes six weeks. Not because it is hard. Because no one can say whose it is, so it travels. Up for comfort, sideways for consensus, into a forum for cover.
Push decisions down without the conditions to hold them there and you get more escalation, not less.
Distributed authority without thresholds is not empowerment, it is exposure with better branding.
A decision belongs with the closest role that can do three things. Bear the consequences. Reach the evidence. Hold real authority to commit, within explicit thresholds.
Escalation by rule is predictable. People can see it coming, prepare for it, and stop treating every hard call as a political event.
Nobody chose that default. It is still a choice. Inaction is a structural decision made by no one, and its consequences land on whoever is closest to the work.
Recurring judgement is fine. Recurring negotiation is the failure.
Authority may exist on paper. Until its bounds, its default and its record are written down, every exercise of it is a negotiation.
